prompt: A duplicate checker compares each position only with later positions. On an input with no duplicates, what does this change compared with comparing every position with every other position?

options.text: It removes repeated and self comparisons, but growth remains quadratic
options.explanation: Correct. A fixed fraction of all-pairs work still grows quadratically.
Each item still has many possible partners; avoiding repeats does not reduce it to one check per item.
With no duplicates, no successful equality test can trigger an early return.

options.text: It makes the inner loop a fixed length
options.explanation: Later positions still depend on both input length and current position.

workedExample: Track the partners of each position. Earlier positions have many later partners, and the final positions have fewer. Avoiding self-pairs and reversed pairs removes redundant checks, but doubling a large input still gives about four times as many pairs.

prompt: A CSV validator compares every pair of rows to detect duplicates. Small test files are fast, but large mostly distinct uploads time out. Which change best addresses the source of growth?

options.explanation: This may let more work finish but leaves the quadratic comparison count.

options.text: Skip comparisons of each row with itself
options.explanation: That removes only a small fraction of work; distinct row pairs still grow quadratically.

options.text: Use sorting plus neighbouring comparisons, or a suitable hash set
options.explanation: Correct. These approaches avoid explicitly checking every pair; choose based on ordering, memory and hashing constraints.

options.text: Assume early exit will make all large files fast
options.explanation: Distinct inputs can still force every pair comparison.

workedExample: Find the repeated work: every new row is compared against many others. A faster machine changes per-comparison cost; a different search structure changes how many comparisons are needed. Sorting groups equal rows, while a set remembers previously seen values under appropriate hashing assumptions.
